entries.change: Added a Method section documenting how papers are found and how one is judged to be a spoken-LLM benchmark: the two arXiv harvests, the scoring formula, the reading pass, the recall pass and the daily crawl, each with the count it produced; the three-part inclusion rule with in/out examples; and the borderline policies. Three files published alongside: the 120 build-day rejections with reasons (data/rejected-2026-08-22.json), the reader notes on borderline calls (data/inclusion-notes-2026-08-22.md), and a ledger of every paper the daily crawl has flagged since launch with its verdict (data/crawl-ledger.json, regenerated by each build).

Added three benchmarks from the 2026-09-09 to 2026-09-10 arXiv window, out of nine mechanically flagged candidates. AudioICL-Bench (SLT 2026, author-reported acceptance; National Taiwan University with MIT) resamples the rule for every episode so no answer is recoverable from pre-trained priors, separating audio Task Learning from Task Recognition across nine tasks on two diagnostic axes; five LALMs bind new labels well when perception is easy but no model exceeds a 7.1% average on the three temporal tasks, and a MorseCode control that supplies the full dictionary and asks for one character still tops out at 11.5%. French Full-Duplex-Bench (EMNLP 2026 Industry Track, author-reported acceptance; Luqia Technologies, Montreal) ports the Full-Duplex-Bench tasks to Canadian and European French from real recordings, and finds that timing-based metrics survive a language switch while user-interruption rating does not; human-human conversations are scored with the same metrics and are not uniformly the best, which is the point. Switch-Aware English-Yoruba Evaluation (preprint; University of Florida) is an evaluation protocol over the existing AfriCodeSwitch corpus: a deterministic 2,000-utterance manifest plus switch-localized metrics showing that aggregate WER hides code-switching behaviour, that Yoruba token error stays at or above 0.97 for almost every system, and that several generative audio LMs exceed 100% WER through translation, verbosity and prompt leakage rather than substitution. Thirty-eight result cells were recorded, each carrying its source table. DeSTA2.5-Audio was added as a model; its builder is left unrecorded because neither the arXiv HTML nor the PDF first page of arXiv 2507.02768 prints an affiliation block. Luqia Technologies is new to the institution map. The remaining six candidates were reviewed and marked out of scope: a multi-sensor gait benchmark, a challenge system description, a low-resource TTS robustness framework, a KV-cache quantization method, a speech-LLM post-training framework and a VAD onset-time evaluation.

Added five benchmarks from the 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-09 arXiv window, out of 21 mechanically flagged candidates. SEA-SpeechBench (EMNLP 2026, accepted) covers 11 Southeast Asian languages over 99 evaluation sets, 97,194 samples and 597 hours, with both English and native-language prompting. ARIA-Rubrics (AACL 2026, accepted) scores the reasoning chain rather than the answer, through six automatic metrics validated against 45 human annotators. S3-Bench (preprint) evaluates speech interaction models as scientific voice assistants over 1,980 spoken queries and 213 multi-turn dialogues in 10 disciplines. Tri-PvP (Findings of EMNLP 2026, accepted) separates modality bias from evidence-form bias across 8,000 tri-modal conflict samples. SA-Bench (NCMMSC 2026, accepted) evaluates speaker-aware timeline recovery and a 15-attribute annotation schema over 8.87 hours. Nineteen result cells were recorded, each carrying its source table. Three institutions were added: Imperial College London, the Technical University of Munich and the Center for AI Safety. The remaining 16 candidates were reviewed and marked out of scope, most because the system under test is a pure ASR, TTS, audio-video generation or text-only model rather than a general spoken LLM.

Combined reviewed metric aliases into 82 groups across 27 benchmarks. Matching scores across at least three common models were followed by source-table checks of quantity, subset and input condition; full-group conflicts block transitive merges. The groups cover 211 source-scoped names and 1,412 observations. Metric options across benchmarks with results decreased from 3,161 to 3,056. All 15,972 original observations are preserved; expanding a table cell shows original names, values, sources and notes, and conflicting unmerged values are all shown. Of 248 stronger candidate pairs reviewed, 167 support approved groups and 81 remain separate. The public audit at metric-aliases.html links every approved group to source tables and records decisions for all 2,379 candidate pairs. This is an AI source audit, not human validation or a new model evaluation.

Acted on a reader's email listing five papers as missing. Two were already here and needed nothing: Llama-Mimi (arXiv 2509.14882) and Flow-SLM (arXiv 2508.09350) were both added earlier the same day. The other three produced three new models and one new benchmark. MoshiRAG (arXiv 2604.12928, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago with Kyutai and Gradium) is a full-duplex speech language model that fires an asynchronous retrieval call while it is still speaking; its 26 scores on Full-Duplex-Bench and Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 were already in the building - the tables had been read for the other models in them - and were dropped only because the model had no id, the same failure that hid Flow-SLM. Bagpiper (arXiv 2602.05220, Carnegie Mellon with LY Corporation and NVIDIA Research) is an 8B unified audio understanding-and-generation model, carrying its three published understanding scores (MMAU-Mini 74.5, AIR-Bench chat 6.57, AudioBench 70.39). AudioCRAG (arXiv 2510.02044, Carnegie Mellon and Meta) is new to the catalogue: CRAG's factual questions re-issued as speech, 1,862 synthetic and 618 human-recorded queries, scoring a speech-in speech-out model on tool-augmented QA against web-search and knowledge-graph APIs. Its 16 accuracy cells name the condition they were measured under - closed book, open book, or the paper's own Streaming RAG method - because those are not the same claim; OpusLM's 0.0 under open book carries the paper's own footnote that the model cannot take tool references in speech-out zero-shot, and OpusLM (arXiv 2506.17611) was added as a model so that row is not another score quoted without a name. Two organisations are new to the map, Gradium in Paris and LY Corporation in Japan. AudioCRAG is recorded as a preprint: arXiv shows no journal-ref, DOI or acceptance comment, and the paper says its human split will be released on acceptance.

Added twelve models that the catalogue had been quoting without naming — Soundwave, Uni-MoE-2.0-Omni, Llama-Mimi, DIFFA, DIFFA-2, InteractiveOmni, Stream-Omni, MGM-Omni, Audio-Omni, SageLM, Falcon3-Audio and AudSemThinker — as 20 rows once size variants are counted separately, carrying 298 scores. They came off the refusal ledger introduced earlier the same day: each appears in at least two independent papers on at least two benchmarks, which an ablation row does not, and each was then checked against its own paper as a real general-purpose audio or speech model rather than a method or a training recipe. Builders were read from each paper's PDF first page, which for several of these carries an affiliation block the arXiv HTML drops; two organisations are new to the map, Maastricht University and the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi. The scores themselves were not retyped: the canonicaliser now has a pattern for each name, so they come through the same variant folding and the same own-paper-wins rule as every other cell.

Daily round: five flagged candidates reviewed, one added. Warmth-Mediated Harm Probe (arXiv 2609.04256, Microsoft Redmond) audits a deployed speech-enabled model on multi-turn mental-health disclosures: 38 scripts built from the WHO mhGAP Intervention Guide across its nine priority presenting conditions, each run over a fixed 7-turn structure ending in a single relational ask, executed twice on Azure OpenAI gpt-realtime in an audio and a text-only arm (532 responses). Twelve result cells are recorded from its Tables 2 and 3 plus Section 4.1, including the finding that at the elicitation turn the model's voice moves away from warmth rather than toward it (duration -4.47 s, speaking rate +0.40 w/s, mean F0 -4.74 Hz, mean energy -1.49 dB, five of seven features p<.001) while transcript-judged acceptance of the ask stays high in both arms (parasocial commitment 0.58 audio vs 0.63 text, McNemar exact p=0.73), and that audio delivery alone costs 3.4 to 5.1 percentage points of MedQA accuracy. Filed as a preprint: arXiv metadata carries no comment, journal-ref or DOI, so no venue is claimed. Four candidates were rejected as out of scope because the systems under test are not general-purpose spoken LLMs: PRISM-Bench (2609.04867) and AVENUE (2609.04253) evaluate text-to-audio-video generation and audio-video editing models, ElderBench (2609.04850) evaluates mobile GUI agents, and TRILOGUE (2609.04452) ships paired audio but says in its own limitations that its baselines run on ASR transcripts and that speech-native audio-language models are left as future work.

Added VoxtLM (arXiv 2309.07937, Carnegie Mellon University and 42dot), a decoder-only model that folds speech recognition, speech synthesis, text generation and speech continuation into one vocabulary of text tokens plus discrete speech tokens. Its own Table 7 reports two 1.3B runs that differ only in training data, and both are listed: sWUGGY 66.1 / sBLIMP 56.7 on the base mixture, and 65.6 / 57.1 with 11M extra paired utterances. VoxtLM had been quoted in six papers in this catalogue under six different spellings and was recognised in none of them, so all fourteen of its cells were discarded. Two things that search turned up and are worth stating: three of those papers print 66.1 / 57.1 for VoxtLM, which pairs the sWUGGY of one run with the sBLIMP of the other, and the numbers above are the paper's own; and the drop had a second cause beyond the spelling — a model appearing in fewer than three tables was filtered out for thinness, which VoxtLM was. Both refusals now land in a written ledger (raw/unmapped_models.json) instead of a count on a terminal.

Added Flow-SLM (arXiv 2508.09350, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago and Stony Brook University) in three variants — 270M, 1B and 1B trained on the extended set — with the 15 scores its paper reports: sWUGGY and sBLIMP on the ZeroSpeech 2021 benchmark (Table I) and acoustic consistency, sentiment alignment and background alignment on SALMon (Table III). Flow-SLM is a textless spoken language model that predicts a semantic token and a continuous acoustic vector at each step with a flow-matching head, instead of handing acoustic detail to a separate vocoder. Two caveats the paper states are carried on every cell: sWUGGY is the all-words split, and only the semantic-token predictor is scored on SALMon because the flow-matching head yields no explicit likelihood. The paper's third results table (generated-speech quality: genPPL, speaker similarity, Fréchet speech distance on LibriSpeech continuations) is its own protocol rather than a catalogued benchmark, so it is not shown here. This entry was already in the citing-paper pool and its tables had been read — every Flow-SLM row was dropped because the model had no id in the roster, which is why a model can be missing from the tables while the paper it comes from is not. Fixed at the same time: Table III's "SpiritLM-exp-7B" row had been recorded against SpiRit-LM rather than SpiRit-LM Expressive.

GPT-6 metadata audit covered all 383 benchmark institution sets and publication records, and all 230 model records. Corrected 13 benchmark institution sets and 8 model builder records. Updated 80 venue records, including 37 status changes plus track and source corrections. Removed the Vox-Profile and MSEB follow-up paper mismatches; separated Audio-AAAI, CVPR Findings and ISMIR LBD from main-conference counts; restored official proceedings missed by stale arXiv comments. Added a complete per-record audit with remaining uncertainties at audit-2026-09-06.html and guarded corrections for regeneration. This AI audit is not human validation.

Added "Where they were published": the publication venue of every catalogue entry, in a new section and on each benchmark record. The catalogue is built from arXiv, so whether a benchmark ever cleared peer review was not answerable from the listing; it was looked up paper by paper against the venues’ own archives. Of the 383 benchmarks, 151 have appeared in proceedings or a journal, 34 are accepted with the meeting still ahead, 195 are preprints with no publication found, and 3 could not be settled. They span 29 venues — ACL, ICASSP and Interspeech the largest — with the reviewed papers split roughly evenly between the ACL-family NLP venues, the speech venues and the machine-learning conferences. Method: candidates from the arXiv journal-ref and author comment, DBLP, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar; the verdict from the venue’s own record (ACL Anthology, ISCA Archive, OpenReview, publisher DOI), quoted and linked. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were never accepted as proof: both name venues before proceedings exist and both get edition years wrong. Every verdict was then re-read mechanically — the evidence link is opened and the paper’s own title checked against it, and a source that did not produce the answer is asked whether it agrees. Only confirmed records are counted; the rest are shown on the entry and excluded from every number. Two failure modes drove the design and are worth recording: papers are retitled between preprint and camera-ready (AV-Odyssey Bench was published as "Probing Audio-Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models through the Lens of Audio"), so title-only matching reports published papers as preprints; and matching on a benchmark’s short name is unsafe — "EMIS" exactly matches a 1998 machine-translation system description in the Anthology. Retitles are now caught by author identity plus a check that the record names the benchmark itself, and short names are never matched. "Accepted" is kept distinct from "published" throughout: Interspeech 2026 had not met when this ran, and the ISCA Archive has no 2026 index, so nothing there is published yet.

Daily review of the 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-03 arXiv candidates: three added, three ruled out of scope. Added DSB-IFEval (DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval, arXiv 2609.03423), a full-duplex benchmark testing whether an agent infers floor-management behaviour from a persona rather than an explicit instruction - 1,038 cases over 240 synthesised conversations, deterministic IAS plus LLM-judged PAS, with 18 result cells for six real-time systems. Added OmniEvaluator (arXiv 2609.01315), an omni-modal evaluation harness, recorded as a harness rather than a data contribution. Added the Generative-Call Decision Test (arXiv 2608.27817), an audit protocol asking whether a generative audio call still changes a closed-set decision once transcript and encoder evidence are available, with three VocalSound accuracies. New model entry F-Actor and new institution NatWest Group; affiliations recorded for all three benchmarks (University of Maryland College Park; NAVER Cloud AI with Korea University, KAIST AI and Seoul National University; National Research Council Canada). Ruled out of scope: a fixed-voice Thai TTS system (2609.03502), the Last Translation Benchmark (2609.04173, a machine-translation benchmark where audio is an optional attachment with no reported audio subset), and a sign-language-translation metric paper (2609.03734).

New section 'Who builds them': every benchmark traced to the institutions on its paper (377 of 380 counted after an independent second read; 408 organisations in 40 countries/territories) and every non-cascade model to its releasing organisation with an evidence link. World map (country totals + institution circles placed at the site the paper names, three counting modes), ranked institutions and countries, academic/company split, lead region by year, organisations in both lists, and an 'Institutions' row on each benchmark record. Affiliations were read from the papers' own author blocks and independently re-checked; canonical names, countries and coordinates were cross-checked against OpenStreetMap and reviewed in three rounds by a second model (Codex), whose corrections are applied. New files: institutions.json, affiliations.json, world.json.

Catalogued AIB (2609.02277), the auditory illusion benchmark for LALMs, with 36 Table 2 average-column cells (HLA / RA / ISI / control accuracy for 8 LALMs plus Gemini 3.1 Pro); Pengi excluded because >20% of its replies were unparseable. Three other flagged candidates ruled out of scope (2609.02343 SonicCaps captioning training dataset, 2609.01788 VakyArth text-only Indic pragmatics, 2609.01810 TalkFa text Farsi dialogue).

Catalogued TAG-Bench (2609.01542) and VoiceLongMemEval (2609.00570) from the 2026-09-03 daily round; added 11 TAG-Bench overall-mIoU cells (Table 2) and 4 VoiceLongMemEval audio-native cells (Table 8). Five other flagged candidates ruled out of scope (2609.00727 probing study, 2609.01315 evaluation harness, 2609.00276 AD-detection classifiers, 2609.00330 text matchers over ASR transcripts, 2609.01113 text MRC).

Six benchmarks added from the 2026-08-28/31 arXiv batch: VocalAffectBench (2608.28932, vocal emotion from audio alone), MusicGroundingBench (2608.29480, temporal music grounding), CREMA-ASIS (2608.28966, acoustic and semantic affective cues put in conflict), HEAR (2608.29120, speaker-attributed reasoning over multi-party audio), a prosodic-heuristic diagnostic for sarcasm detection (2608.30204), and AynVQA from the ImageEval 2026 shared task (2608.30475, spoken VQA in English and Modern Standard Arabic). 29 sourced result cells and three models (Step-Audio 2 mini, Gemma-4-E4B-it, GPT-Realtime 2) were added with them. VocalAffectBench cells are read off v2 of that paper, which revised the clip count and the headline accuracy downward from v1. Four further flagged papers were reviewed and left out of scope: TEMPO (2608.29999) and stride-k subsampling (2608.30927) propose a model and a method rather than a benchmark, VoiceCodeBench (2608.28916) evaluates twelve ASR systems and no general spoken LLM, and MusGU+ (2608.30940) evaluates generative music systems.

Three benchmarks added from the 2026-08-27/28 arXiv batch: SURE-Challenge (2608.27783, pre-generation rejection of audio that carries no evidence), MuSP-Bench (2608.28212, music understanding across scores and performances), and DualEvasion (2608.28040, textual evasion vs. vocal confidence in earnings calls). 29 sourced result cells and three models (Qwen-Audio-Chat, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Muse Spark 1.2) added with them. Three further flagged papers were reviewed and left out of scope.

Disclosure strengthened at the owner's request: the site now states plainly, in the hero and the footer, that it is not an official publication of ISCA or any other body, that no human has verified its content, and that it is the output of Hung-yi Lee casually prompting an AI agent (Claude Fable 5) to see what AI agents can do. Also added the SCOOT 2.0 cross-links and the stats.json feed earlier the same day.

Two corrections to the overview paper, caught by an adversarial fact-check while preparing tutorial material from it. Section 5.6 claimed eight of the nine most-measured models are open-weight; the correct count is seven of nine (Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4o-Audio are API-served, without released weights). Section 7.3 called the most-measured system in the catalogue a 2024 model, contradicting section 5.6's own tally: the most-measured is Qwen2.5-Omni (tech report posted March 2025); the 2024 Qwen2-Audio is second. Catalogue data is unaffected - both errors were in the paper's prose only.

Daily review: nine flagged papers read, two catalogued. AudioSpan (arXiv 2608.26431) pairs 360 in-the-wild recordings of 10 minutes to 2.7 hours - each also released in an anchor-modified version - with 3,240 items split across perception, understanding and reasoning, and scores them three ways: multiple choice, rubric-graded open-ended, and an anchor chain cut off at the first error. MMI (arXiv 2608.26317) tests whether an omni model returns the right output modality at all across text, image, audio, video and document, with audio the hardest of the five. They contribute 36 and 15 result cells respectively. AudioSpan cells are the Avg columns of Table 3 and are recorded only for rows where the model name is printed on the row itself, since the table's grouped standard/thinking pairs leave the unnamed rows ambiguous; every cell is labelled with the model's thinking configuration and audio input limit, because open models are scored on truncated audio while closed models run untruncated. MMI cells are Table 4 and record MPS, pass rate and input failure rate rather than the MMI Value, which the paper defines but leaves untested because too few assets came back to grade. Eight models added to the registry. The other seven papers were ruled out of scope: two benchmark audio-video generation, one is a code-switched ASR benchmark, one evaluates unsupervised speech units, one is a mechanistic analysis with no benchmark, one proposes a retrieval embedder, and SpeechGym is an RL training environment that reuses an existing text benchmark's tasks and evaluator unchanged.

Daily review: one benchmark catalogued from three flagged papers. TurnBench (arXiv 2608.25218) pairs a 30-hour, triple-annotated corpus of 154 dyadic conversations with a standardised protocol for end-of-turn and interruption detection, and makes conversation type a controlled variable across six interaction styles; it contributes 18 result cells read off the Overall pooled test columns of Table IV. Only the three deployed spoken-LLM systems in that table are recorded - Gemini 3.1 Flash Live and Moshi, scored on end-of-turn only because a full-duplex model's decisions are read off its produced audio, and the two endpointing modes of the gpt-realtime API, whose cells are labelled by mode and noted as a component of the deployed API rather than the model's own speech. The remaining eleven baselines are energy VADs, endpointing heads and trained turn-taking predictors, not general spoken LLMs, so they are left in the paper. One new model entry was needed (Gemini 3.1 Flash Live). Full-duplex latency is not comparable with a predictor's decision latency because it includes response generation, which is recorded in the benchmark note. Two further flagged papers were read and ruled out of scope: a logit-lens interpretability study of Qwen3-Omni's middle layers (2608.24958), which states outright that its quantities are controls rather than benchmark scores, and Flower Hub (2608.25114), a federated-learning benchmarking platform with no speech or audio content at all.

Daily review: two benchmarks catalogued from four flagged papers. EXAM2 (arXiv 2608.23758) is a six-language multiple-choice audio-understanding set of 5,667 questions in which every answer choice also exists as a generated image, letting the same items be scored on audio, on images, on transcripts or on combinations; it contributes 20 result cells read off Table 3 (the raw-audio rows only, averaged over the six languages), and its test split is derived from MMAU-test-mini so scores are not independent of MMAU. LongAudioQA (arXiv 2608.24048) is a 16,456-question set over long meeting audio from AliMeeting, AMI and DailyTalk with a five-way question taxonomy including an acoustic-aware split that a transcript cannot answer; it contributes 45 result cells from the 'Speech as Context' block of Table 3. LongAudioQA is introduced alongside a method (GRGA) by the same authors, which is recorded in its note - every number on it so far comes from the paper that proposed it. Two further flagged papers were ruled out of scope: a human-versus-LLM-judge agreement study for voice agents (2608.24314), which proposes no benchmark of its own and scores text judges rather than spoken LLMs, and FireRedAudio (2608.24168), which is a unified audio language model rather than an evaluation. No model entries were needed; all eight evaluated systems were already in the model table.

Daily review: two benchmarks catalogued. MRMAD (arXiv 2608.22236) tests whether audio-language models can hear how audio is degraded - nine degradation types at three severities across speech, music and sound, posed as multi-turn dialogues over multiple clips - and contributes 66 result cells read off Table 4 for 22 systems. PUMA (arXiv 2608.21853) is a Polish benchmark whose three audio categories (ASR, speech QA, sound and music QA) contribute 36 strict-score cells from Table 1; for the same-family model pairs the audio columns are recorded against the audio member. Twelve new model entries were needed. Nine further flagged papers were read and ruled out of scope: a coding-agent game-development benchmark, a KV-cache method for long-form speech LLMs, a LoRA post-training study on DCASE audio QA, two video benchmarks (Southeast Asian cultural moments, Hollywood narrative understanding) where audio is an auxiliary condition for vision models rather than the object of evaluation, a text-only Bengali safety benchmark, an ASR-error study of multi-hop RAG pipelines, a clinical on-device meeting-summarisation system, and an audio deepfake detection challenge.

Daily review: OmniAssistBench (arXiv 2608.21360) catalogued, with 11 overall-average result cells read off Tables 2 and 3 and three new model entries (Doubao-Seed-2.0-lite, MiniCPM-o-4.5, Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus). It evaluates omni-modal LLMs as real-time video assistants whose user instructions arrive as audio embedded in the test video. Five further flagged papers were read and ruled out of scope: a Chinese abusive-language benchmark over text rather than speech, a multi-turn conversational AI survey, an audio-chapterization training method, a shared-task system description, and a debate-practice HCI system. Separately, the crawler window was widened after three consecutive empty days: arXiv makes a submission searchable several days after its submittedDate, so a three-day window could close before a paper became visible. Six papers recovered from that gap are included in this review.

Corrections from an external data audit, each re-checked against the current arXiv version before applying. AudioTrust: 26 fairness cells showed 1-Gamma under the published Gamma symbol, which reversed the model ordering; the printed Gamma values are restored and the column now states that higher is fairer. Nine result values had gone stale as their source papers were revised (VCB Bench Fun-Audio-Chat GK and ML, OmniBench MIO-Instruct across three settings, SpeechRole Qwen2.5-Omni and GPT-4o-Audio in both languages), and Fun-Audio-Chat's MTD score, absent from the earlier version, is now recorded. 87 cells pointed at table numbers that had shifted under unversioned arXiv links (VCB Bench, OmniBench, OpenOmni, AudioMarathon); locators are corrected and now name the version they were checked against.

Scale-collision guard rewritten. It had been splitting any metric whose values spanned 10 and 50 into '0-10 scale' and '0-100 scale' columns, which mislabelled accuracy, WER, F1, exact-match and rate metrics where a low number is simply a low score: 1,251 cells carried a scale the source never states. A split now requires seeing one model reported at both magnitudes by two different sources, and never applies to a metric published as a percentage. 166 cells across 11 metrics still split; the rest read as their papers printed them.

Daily review: two flagged arXiv candidates read in full and both ruled out of scope. arXiv:2608.19936 probes benchmark optimization in ASR transcription, and arXiv:2608.20326 is a confidence-estimation method for music information retrieval; neither evaluates general-purpose spoken LLMs. Catalogue unchanged at 360 benchmarks.

Results now include papers that USE each benchmark, not only the paper that introduced it. All 1,619 citing papers on arXiv were read; 509 of them (31%) actually ran a catalogued benchmark, the rest only cite it in prose. Tables: 2,433 to 15,220 sourced cells over 197 models and 686 distinct source papers, with 341 of 360 benchmarks now carrying at least one score. Surveys were skipped so every number stays first-hand.

Extraction extended to every catalogued benchmark paper, not just the well-known ones: 268 further papers read. Benchmarks with at least one sourced score went from 90 to 327 of 360, and the tables from 2,913 to 7,858 cells over 179 models. Model-name matching now tolerates spacing variants (Qwen 2.5 Omni = Qwen2.5-Omni).

Second registry audit after the SALMon report. Found a silent Unicode fault: papers using U+2011 non-breaking hyphens (SpeechR) produced model names that looked identical to matched ones but never matched, dropping every row. Also recovered Gemini variants, J-Moshi, Megrez-3B-Omni, Grok, Fun-Audio-Chat and others, gave each named cascade pipeline its own row instead of discarding it, and explicitly excluded CLAP/VAD/encoder/TTS rows that are out of scope. Dropped cells fell from 1,031 to 263; the tables gained 480 cells and 70 models.

Presentation: the full catalogue moved to the foot of the page and is now one line per benchmark, paged. Result tables open at 6 benchmarks by 12 models with controls to widen, and a column whose benchmark reports several metrics now carries a metric picker instead of silently showing one.

Fixed a model-registry gap that silently dropped the pure speech-LM family (TWIST, LAST, pGSLM, dGSLM, GSLM, AudioLM, Spectron, SpiRit-LM Expressive) — the family that likelihood-based benchmarks actually evaluate. SALMon went from 1 model to 8; 152 result cells and 17 models recovered overall.
Recall pass over an independently harvested arXiv pool (25,446 speech-relevant records via OAI-PMH) added 91 benchmarks that keyword-driven discovery had missed.
Result tables constrained to one metric per column, with a scale-collision guard that separates 1-5 judge scores from the same metric normalised to 100.
Atlas published: 360 benchmarks, 19 capability categories, arXiv timeline, and model-by-benchmark tables with 2,433 sourced result cells.
